claim: Dnmt3a is the sole 'writer' of atypical non-CpG methylation (mCH) in the brain.
source: In the brain, Dnmt3a is the sole 'writer' of atypical non-CpG methylation (mCH), and MeCP2 is the only known 'reader' for mCH.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: MeCP2 is the only known 'reader' for mCH in the brain.
source: In the brain, Dnmt3a is the sole 'writer' of atypical non-CpG methylation (mCH), and MeCP2 is the only known 'reader' for mCH.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Loss of Dnmt3a causes global loss of mCH in GABAergic inhibitory neurons.
source: Loss of Dnmt3a causes global loss of mCH and a subset of mCG sites resulting in more widespread transcriptional alterations and severe neurological dysfunction than MeCP2 loss.
evidence: This is supported by methylation sequencing data showing ~90% loss of mCH in Dnmt3a cKO neurons.

claim: Loss of Dnmt3a causes loss of a subset of mCG sites in GABAergic inhibitory neurons.
source: Loss of Dnmt3a causes global loss of mCH and a subset of mCG sites resulting in more widespread transcriptional alterations and severe neurological dysfunction than MeCP2 loss.
evidence: This is supported by methylation sequencing data showing ~10% loss of mCG in Dnmt3a cKO neurons.

claim: Loss of Dnmt3a results in more widespread transcriptional alterations than MeCP2 loss in GABAergic inhibitory neurons.
source: Loss of Dnmt3a causes global loss of mCH and a subset of mCG sites resulting in more widespread transcriptional alterations and severe neurological dysfunction than MeCP2 loss.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing more differentially expressed genes in Dnmt3a cKO compared to Mecp2 cKO.

claim: Loss of Dnmt3a results in more severe neurological dysfunction than MeCP2 loss in GABAergic inhibitory neurons.
source: Loss of Dnmt3a causes global loss of mCH and a subset of mCG sites resulting in more widespread transcriptional alterations and severe neurological dysfunction than MeCP2 loss.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing more severe phenotypes in Dnmt3a cKO mice.

claim: MeCP2 is responsible for reading only part of the Dnmt3a dependent methylation in the brain.
source: These data suggest that MeCP2 is responsible for reading only part of the Dnmt3a dependent methylation in the brain.
evidence: This is supported by the finding that only ~12% of DEGs in Dnmt3a cKO are also significantly altered in Mecp2 cKO.

claim: The impact of MeCP2 on genes differentially expressed in both models shows a strong dependence on mCH.
source: Importantly, the impact of MeCP2 on genes differentially expressed in both models shows a strong dependence on mCH, but not Dnmt3a dependent mCG, consistent with mCH playing a central role in the pathogenesis of Rett Syndrome.
evidence: This is supported by integrative analysis showing significant correlation between gene expression changes and mCH loss but not mCG loss in common DEGs.

claim: The impact of MeCP2 on genes differentially expressed in both models does not show dependence on Dnmt3a dependent mCG.
source: Importantly, the impact of MeCP2 on genes differentially expressed in both models shows a strong dependence on mCH, but not Dnmt3a dependent mCG, consistent with mCH playing a central role in the pathogenesis of Rett Syndrome.
evidence: This is supported by integrative analysis showing no significant correlation between gene expression changes and mCG loss in common DEGs.

claim: mCH plays a central role in the pathogenesis of Rett Syndrome.
source: Importantly, the impact of MeCP2 on genes differentially expressed in both models shows a strong dependence on mCH, but not Dnmt3a dependent mCG, consistent with mCH playing a central role in the pathogenesis of Rett Syndrome.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong dependence of MeCP2-regulated genes on mCH.

claim: DNA methylation was described by Rollin Hotchkiss in 1948.
source: Although DNA methylation in mammals was described by Rollin Hotchkiss in 1948 (Hotchkiss, 1948), it took nearly thirty years to realize its function in the regulation of gene expression to shape fundamental biological processes including cell differentiation, genomic imprinting and genome stability (Compere and Palmiter, 1981; Li and Zhang, 2014).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation.

claim: DNA methylation functions in the regulation of gene expression to shape fundamental biological processes including cell differentiation, genomic imprinting and genome stability.
source: Although DNA methylation in mammals was described by Rollin Hotchkiss in 1948 (Hotchkiss, 1948), it took nearly thirty years to realize its function in the regulation of gene expression to shape fundamental biological processes including cell differentiation, genomic imprinting and genome stability (Compere and Palmiter, 1981; Li and Zhang, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established research.

claim: DNA methylation is functionally dynamic.
source: Rather than static and solely repressive to gene expression, DNA methylation is functionally dynamic (Shen et al., 2014), and in some cases has been shown to activate gene expression (Aran et al., 2011; Ball et al., 2009; Hellman and Chess, 2007; Keown et al., 2017) highlighting that context and protein factors that recognize methylated cytosine can alter the transcriptional outcome of this epigenetic mark.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shen et al., 2014.

claim: DNA methylation has been shown to activate gene expression in some cases.
source: Rather than static and solely repressive to gene expression, DNA methylation is functionally dynamic (Shen et al., 2014), and in some cases has been shown to activate gene expression (Aran et al., 2011; Ball et al., 2009; Hellman and Chess, 2007; Keown et al., 2017) highlighting that context and protein factors that recognize methylated cytosine can alter the transcriptional outcome of this epigenetic mark.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Context and protein factors that recognize methylated cytosine can alter the transcriptional outcome of DNA methylation.
source: Rather than static and solely repressive to gene expression, DNA methylation is functionally dynamic (Shen et al., 2014), and in some cases has been shown to activate gene expression (Aran et al., 2011; Ball et al., 2009; Hellman and Chess, 2007; Keown et al., 2017) highlighting that context and protein factors that recognize methylated cytosine can alter the transcriptional outcome of this epigenetic mark.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited evidence showing variable effects of methylation.

claim: Non-CpG methylation (mCH) is not found in most mammalian cells.
source: This non-CpG methylation (also known as mCH, where H equals A, C or T) is not found in most mammalian cells but has been detected in pluripotent cells (Lister et al., 2009; Ramsahoye et al., 2000), some human tissues (Schultz et al., 2015), and is enriched in postnatal neurons (He and Ecker, 2015; Lister et al., 2013; Price et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations showing restricted distribution of mCH.

claim: mCH has been detected in pluripotent cells.
source: This non-CpG methylation (also known as mCH, where H equals A, C or T) is not found in most mammalian cells but has been detected in pluripotent cells (Lister et al., 2009; Ramsahoye et al., 2000), some human tissues (Schultz et al., 2015), and is enriched in postnatal neurons (He and Ecker, 2015; Lister et al., 2013; Price et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lister et al., 2009 and Ramsahoye et al., 2000.

claim: mCH has been detected in some human tissues.
source: This non-CpG methylation (also known as mCH, where H equals A, C or T) is not found in most mammalian cells but has been detected in pluripotent cells (Lister et al., 2009; Ramsahoye et al., 2000), some human tissues (Schultz et al., 2015), and is enriched in postnatal neurons (He and Ecker, 2015; Lister et al., 2013; Price et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schultz et al., 2015.

claim: mCH is enriched in postnatal neurons.
source: This non-CpG methylation (also known as mCH, where H equals A, C or T) is not found in most mammalian cells but has been detected in pluripotent cells (Lister et al., 2009; Ramsahoye et al., 2000), some human tissues (Schultz et al., 2015), and is enriched in postnatal neurons (He and Ecker, 2015; Lister et al., 2013; Price et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The mCH mark increases in neurons predominantly after birth.
source: The mCH mark increases in neurons predominantly after birth and is concurrent with the period of peak synaptogenesis throughout the first 25 years of life in humans (or the first 4 weeks in mice).
evidence: This is supported by the timing information provided and citations in the manuscript.

claim: The increase in mCH is concurrent with the period of peak synaptogenesis throughout the first 25 years of life in humans.
source: The mCH mark increases in neurons predominantly after birth and is concurrent with the period of peak synaptogenesis throughout the first 25 years of life in humans (or the first 4 weeks in mice).
evidence: This is a temporal correlation stated in the text.

claim: The increase in mCH is concurrent with the period of peak synaptogenesis throughout the first 4 weeks in mice.
source: The mCH mark increases in neurons predominantly after birth and is concurrent with the period of peak synaptogenesis throughout the first 25 years of life in humans (or the first 4 weeks in mice).
evidence: This is a temporal correlation stated in the text.

claim: The resulting mCH pattern is largely conserved between mice and humans.
source: The resulting mCH pattern is largely conserved between mice and humans, where it makes up a high percentage of all DNA methylation in neurons (He and Ecker, 2015; Lister et al., 2013; He et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: mCH makes up a high percentage of all DNA methylation in neurons.
source: The resulting mCH pattern is largely conserved between mice and humans, where it makes up a high percentage of all DNA methylation in neurons (He and Ecker, 2015; Lister et al., 2013; He et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: DNA methylation is catalyzed by de novo DNA methyltransferases Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b in mammals.
source: In mammals, DNA methylation is catalyzed by de novo DNA methyltransferases Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b, and maintained by Dnmt1 in the CpG context (Jurkowska and Jeltsch, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: DNA methylation is maintained by Dnmt1 in the CpG context in mammals.
source: In mammals, DNA methylation is catalyzed by de novo DNA methyltransferases Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b, and maintained by Dnmt1 in the CpG context (Jurkowska and Jeltsch, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Dnmt3a is the sole 'writer' of mCH in postnatal neurons.
source: Recent studies have shown that Dnmt3a is the sole 'writer' of mCH in postnatal neurons (Lister et al., 2013; Gabel et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2014; Stroud et al., 2017), where it is preferentially found in the CAC nucleotide context (He and Ecker, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: mCH is preferentially found in the CAC nucleotide context in postnatal neurons.
source: Recent studies have shown that Dnmt3a is the sole 'writer' of mCH in postnatal neurons (Lister et al., 2013; Gabel et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2014; Stroud et al., 2017), where it is preferentially found in the CAC nucleotide context (He and Ecker, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to He and Ecker, 2015.

claim: Mutations in DNMT3A have been associated with disorders of neurodevelopment.
source: Mutations in DNMT3A have recently been associated with disorders of neurodevelopment (Tatton-Brown et al., 2014; Sanders et al., 2015; Heyn et al., 2019) suggesting that the mechanism by which Dnmt3a dependent methylation is written and read by other protein factors to regulate gene expression is critical for brain maturation.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Loss of function of MeCP2 has been associated with Rett syndrome (RTT).
source: Loss of function of the only known 'reader' of mCH in the mammalian brain, Methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) (Gabel et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015), has long been associated with Rett syndrome (RTT) (Amir et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RTT is an X-linked, postnatal neurological disorder.
source: RTT is an X-linked, postnatal neurological disorder; affected children are apparently healthy for the first 6–18 months of life, then lose their acquired milestones and develop a range of dysfunctions of the central and autonomic nervous systems (Leonard et al., 2017; Zoghbi, 2016).
evidence: This is a clinical description supported by citations.

claim: Affected children with RTT are apparently healthy for the first 6–18 months of life.
source: RTT is an X-linked, postnatal neurological disorder; affected children are apparently healthy for the first 6–18 months of life, then lose their acquired milestones and develop a range of dysfunctions of the central and autonomic nervous systems (Leonard et al., 2017; Zoghbi, 2016).
evidence: This is a clinical description supported by citations.

claim: Children with RTT lose their acquired milestones after 6-18 months of life.
source: RTT is an X-linked, postnatal neurological disorder; affected children are apparently healthy for the first 6–18 months of life, then lose their acquired milestones and develop a range of dysfunctions of the central and autonomic nervous systems (Leonard et al., 2017; Zoghbi, 2016).
evidence: This is a clinical description supported by citations.

claim: Children with RTT develop a range of dysfunctions of the central and autonomic nervous systems.
source: RTT is an X-linked, postnatal neurological disorder; affected children are apparently healthy for the first 6–18 months of life, then lose their acquired milestones and develop a range of dysfunctions of the central and autonomic nervous systems (Leonard et al., 2017; Zoghbi, 2016).
evidence: This is a clinical description supported by citations.

claim: Mouse models of MECP2 mutations in female mice faithfully recapitulate patient symptoms.
source: Mouse models of MECP2 mutations in female mice faithfully recapitulate patient symptoms, the severity of which, in humans and mice, is determined by the specific mutation and the pattern of X-inactivation (Leonard et al., 2017; Young and Zoghbi, 2004; Lombardi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The severity of RTT symptoms in humans and mice is determined by the specific mutation and the pattern of X-inactivation.
source: Mouse models of MECP2 mutations in female mice faithfully recapitulate patient symptoms, the severity of which, in humans and mice, is determined by the specific mutation and the pattern of X-inactivation (Leonard et al., 2017; Young and Zoghbi, 2004; Lombardi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Numerous conditional knockout mice have revealed the importance of MeCP2 function in different cell populations in the brain.
source: Numerous conditional knockout mice have revealed the importance of MeCP2 function in different cell populations in the brain as well as the etiology of RTT symptoms (Chen et al., 2001; Gemelli et al., 2006; Fyffe et al., 2008; Samaco et al., 2009; Chao et al., 2010; Ito-Ishida et al., 2015; Meng et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Goffin et al., 2014; Ward et al., 2011; Adachi et al., 2009; Guy et al., 2001; Su et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations.

claim: MECP2 mutations have been linked to neuropsychiatric conditions beyond RTT.
source: Given the apparent need of every neural cell type for MeCP2, it is not surprising that MECP2 mutations have been linked to other neuropsychiatric conditions beyond RTT (Zoghbi, 2016; Lombardi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Re-expression of MeCP2 in the central nervous system rescues severe neurological symptoms and the prematurely lethal phenotype of constitutive null male mice.
source: Yet re-expression of MeCP2 in the central nervous system (Ross et al., 2016) rescues even the severe neurological symptoms and the prematurely lethal phenotype of constitutive null male mice (Chen et al., 2001; Guy et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: RTT is driven by the loss of MeCP2 function in the nervous system.
source: RTT is thus driven by the loss of MeCP2 function in the nervous system, which continues to be essential into adulthood (McGraw et al., 2011; Cheval et al., 2012), but the underlying architecture is sufficiently intact to support functional rescue.
evidence: This is inferred from rescue experiments and supported by citations.

claim: MeCP2 function continues to be essential into adulthood.
source: RTT is thus driven by the loss of MeCP2 function in the nervous system, which continues to be essential into adulthood (McGraw et al., 2011; Cheval et al., 2012), but the underlying architecture is sufficiently intact to support functional rescue.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: MeCP2 binds to mCH at genes that are misregulated in Mecp2 knockout brains.
source: The recent finding that MeCP2 binds to mCH at genes that are misregulated in Mecp2 knockout brains, and that mCH deposition occurs predominantly after birth in conjunction with neuronal maturation, has led to the hypothesis that failure of mutant MeCP2 to bind to mCH could account for the postnatal onset of RTT symptoms (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: mCH deposition occurs predominantly after birth in conjunction with neuronal maturation.
source: The recent finding that MeCP2 binds to mCH at genes that are misregulated in Mecp2 knockout brains, and that mCH deposition occurs predominantly after birth in conjunction with neuronal maturation, has led to the hypothesis that failure of mutant MeCP2 to bind to mCH could account for the postnatal onset of RTT symptoms (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: Failure of mutant MeCP2 to bind to mCH could account for the postnatal onset of RTT symptoms.
source: The recent finding that MeCP2 binds to mCH at genes that are misregulated in Mecp2 knockout brains, and that mCH deposition occurs predominantly after birth in conjunction with neuronal maturation, has led to the hypothesis that failure of mutant MeCP2 to bind to mCH could account for the postnatal onset of RTT symptoms (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: Both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice were born healthy.
source: Both cKO mice were born healthy but started to display symptoms around the time of weaning.
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral experiments.

claim: Both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice started to display symptoms around the time of weaning.
source: Both cKO mice were born healthy but started to display symptoms around the time of weaning.
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral experiments.

claim: Both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice developed hind limb spasticity.
source: Both cKO mice first developed hind limb spasticity (Figure 1A), and by six weeks both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice displayed obsessive grooming (Figure 1B), forepaw apraxia (Figure 1C), muscle weakness (Figure 1D), and motor deficits (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral testing data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: By six weeks both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice displayed obsessive grooming.
source: Both cKO mice first developed hind limb spasticity (Figure 1A), and by six weeks both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice displayed obsessive grooming (Figure 1B), forepaw apraxia (Figure 1C), muscle weakness (Figure 1D), and motor deficits (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral testing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: By six weeks both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice displayed forepaw apraxia.
source: Both cKO mice first developed hind limb spasticity (Figure 1A), and by six weeks both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice displayed obsessive grooming (Figure 1B), forepaw apraxia (Figure 1C), muscle weakness (Figure 1D), and motor deficits (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral testing data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: By six weeks both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice displayed muscle weakness.
source: Both cKO mice first developed hind limb spasticity (Figure 1A), and by six weeks both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice displayed obsessive grooming (Figure 1B), forepaw apraxia (Figure 1C), muscle weakness (Figure 1D), and motor deficits (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral testing data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: By six weeks both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice displayed motor deficits.
source: Both cKO mice first developed hind limb spasticity (Figure 1A), and by six weeks both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice displayed obsessive grooming (Figure 1B), forepaw apraxia (Figure 1C), muscle weakness (Figure 1D), and motor deficits (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral testing data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice showed hippocampal-dependent learning and memory deficits.
source: We found hippocampal-dependent, but not amygdala-dependent, learning and memory deficits (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by fear conditioning data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice did not show amygdala-dependent learning and memory deficits.
source: We found hippocampal-dependent, but not amygdala-dependent, learning and memory deficits (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by fear conditioning data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Starting at 7 to 8 weeks of age, the obsessive grooming led to skin lesions in both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice.
source: Starting at 7 to 8 weeks of age, the obsessive grooming led to skin lesions (Figure 1G); this self-injury was previously observed in Mecp2 cKO mice on an F1 hybrid background (Chao et al., 2010) but was exacerbated on the C57BL/6J background, creating a need for humane euthanasia (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Self-injury was previously observed in Mecp2 cKO mice on an F1 hybrid background.
source: Starting at 7 to 8 weeks of age, the obsessive grooming led to skin lesions (Figure 1G); this self-injury was previously observed in Mecp2 cKO mice on an F1 hybrid background (Chao et al., 2010) but was exacerbated on the C57BL/6J background, creating a need for humane euthanasia (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chao et al., 2010.

claim: Self-injury was exacerbated on the C57BL/6J background in Mecp2 cKO mice.
source: Starting at 7 to 8 weeks of age, the obsessive grooming led to skin lesions (Figure 1G); this self-injury was previously observed in Mecp2 cKO mice on an F1 hybrid background (Chao et al., 2010) but was exacerbated on the C57BL/6J background, creating a need for humane euthanasia (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral experiments.

claim: Both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice still responded to pain stimuli.
source: Both cKO mouse models still responded to pain stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–H), albeit to a lesser degree than controls.
evidence: This is supported by hot plate and tail flick testing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–H.

claim: Both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO mice responded to pain stimuli to a lesser degree than controls.
source: Both cKO mouse models still responded to pain stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–H), albeit to a lesser degree than controls.
evidence: This is supported by hot plate and tail flick testing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–H.

claim: Both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO models show similar alterations in miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents amplitude in the dorsal striatum.
source: We observed decreased amplitude, as well as similar changes in frequency and charge (Figure 1H–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2K–L).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1H–I.

claim: Both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO models show similar changes in miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents frequency in the dorsal striatum.
source: We observed decreased amplitude, as well as similar changes in frequency and charge (Figure 1H–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2K–L).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2K.

claim: Both Dnmt3a cKO and Mecp2 cKO models show similar changes in miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents charge in the dorsal striatum.
source: We observed decreased amplitude, as well as similar changes in frequency and charge (Figure 1H–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2K–L).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2L.

claim: Dnmt3a cKO mice were smaller than control mice starting at weaning age and throughout adulthood.
source: Dnmt3a cKO mice were smaller than control mice starting at weaning age and throughout adulthood (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Forepaw stereotypies were evident in Dnmt3a cKO mice but not the Mecp2 cKO mice on the C57BL/6J background.
source: Forepaw stereotypies were evident in Dnmt3a cKO mice but not the Mecp2 cKO mice on the C57BL/6J background (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1—video 1.

claim: Loss of Dnmt3a in inhibitory neurons led to an increased acoustic startle response.
source: Loss of Dnmt3a in inhibitory neurons led to an increased acoustic startle response (Figure 1K), with loss of MeCP2 in the same cell type showing the opposite trend, similar to a previous MeCP2 study (Chao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by acoustic startle response data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Loss of MeCP2 in inhibitory neurons showed the opposite trend in acoustic startle response compared to Dnmt3a cKO.
source: Loss of Dnmt3a in inhibitory neurons led to an increased acoustic startle response (Figure 1K), with loss of MeCP2 in the same cell type showing the opposite trend, similar to a previous MeCP2 study (Chao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by acoustic startle response data shown in Figure 1K and citation to Chao et al., 2010.

claim: Only the Mecp2 cKO mice developed motor incoordination.
source: Only the Mecp2 cKO mice developed motor incoordination (Figure 1L) and showed a trend for increased sensorimotor gating (Figure 1—figure supplement 2O).
evidence: This is supported by parallel rod footslip data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Only the Mecp2 cKO mice showed a trend for increased sensorimotor gating.
source: Only the Mecp2 cKO mice developed motor incoordination (Figure 1L) and showed a trend for increased sensorimotor gating (Figure 1—figure supplement 2O).
evidence: This is supported by prepulse inhibition data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2O.

claim: Dnmt3a cKO mice showed deficits in conditioned fear training.
source: Dnmt3a cKO mice also showed deficits in conditioned fear training (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by fear conditioning training data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The Dnmt3a cKO mice showed much more severe self-injury, requiring humane euthanasia 2.5 week earlier than Mecp2 cKO mice.
source: Finally, the Dnmt3a cKO mice showed much more severe self-injury, requiring humane euthanasia 2.5 week earlier than Mecp2 cKO mice (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: Methylation was stable in the absence of MeCP2.
source: We found that methylation was stable in the absence of MeCP2 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but ~90% of mCH was lost in the absence of Dnmt3a (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by methylation sequencing data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ~90% of mCH was lost in the absence of Dnmt3a in striatal inhibitory neurons.
source: We found that methylation was stable in the absence of MeCP2 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but ~90% of mCH was lost in the absence of Dnmt3a (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by methylation sequencing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ~10% of mCG was lost in Dnmt3a cKO neurons.
source: We also noted a ~ 10% loss of mCG in Dnmt3a cKO neurons (Figure 2D) consistent with partial mCG demethylation in the prenatal period followed by re-methylation later in development (He et al., 2017; Stroud et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by methylation sequencing data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Dnmt3a is required to re-methylate mCG sites in the postnatal period.
source: Dnmt3a is thus required to re-methylate mCG sites in the postnatal period.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of mCG loss in Dnmt3a cKO and citations showing prenatal demethylation.

claim: mCH and mCG in wild-type mice showed poor genome-wide correlation.
source: While mCH and mCG in wild-type mice showed poor genome-wide correlation (Figure 2E), Dnmt3a dependent mCH and mCG showed significant correlation suggesting that the writing of mCH and mCG are coupled (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Dnmt3a dependent mCH and mCG showed significant correlation.
source: While mCH and mCG in wild-type mice showed poor genome-wide correlation (Figure 2E), Dnmt3a dependent mCH and mCG showed significant correlation suggesting that the writing of mCH and mCG are coupled (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The writing of mCH and mCG are coupled.
source: While mCH and mCG in wild-type mice showed poor genome-wide correlation (Figure 2E), Dnmt3a dependent mCH and mCG showed significant correlation suggesting that the writing of mCH and mCG are coupled (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is inferred from the significant correlation between Dnmt3a dependent mCH and mCG.

claim: Hundreds of genes were differentially expressed in Dnmt3a cKO striatal inhibitory neurons.
source: Comparing gene expression by RNA-Seq for both cKO models, we found hundreds of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), either up- or down-regulated (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Hundreds of genes were differentially expressed in Mecp2 cKO striatal inhibitory neurons.
source: Comparing gene expression by RNA-Seq for both cKO models, we found hundreds of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), either up- or down-regulated (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ~40% of DEGs in the Mecp2 cKO mice were significantly altered in Dnmt3a cKO mice.
source: Although a large portion of DEGs in the Mecp2 cKO mice (~40%) were significantly altered in Dnmt3a cKO mice indicating a dependence on Dnmt3a and an important contribution to RTT, we were surprised to find that only a small percentage of DEGs in the Dnmt3a cKO mice (~12%) were significantly altered in Mecp2 cKO mice (i.e. are 'MeCP2 dependent') (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only ~12% of DEGs in the Dnmt3a cKO mice were significantly altered in Mecp2 cKO mice.
source: Although a large portion of DEGs in the Mecp2 cKO mice (~40%) were significantly altered in Dnmt3a cKO mice indicating a dependence on Dnmt3a and an important contribution to RTT, we were surprised to find that only a small percentage of DEGs in the Dnmt3a cKO mice (~12%) were significantly altered in Mecp2 cKO mice (i.e. are 'MeCP2 dependent') (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: DEGs common to both cKO models changed in the same direction and to a similar degree.
source: Plotting the log2 fold-change in gene expression for each model against one another (Figure 3C), we found that DEGs common to both cKO models changed in the same direction and to a similar degree, consistent with an equal dependence on Dnmt3a and MeCP2.
evidence: This is supported by log2 fold-change correlation analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: DEGs have greater gene body mCH than genes that are unchanged.
source: Plotting gene body mCH in wild-type mice for each category of differentially expressed genes, we find that, overall, DEGs have greater gene body mCH than genes that are unchanged, with up-regulated genes having higher mCH levels than down-regulated genes (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by gene body methylation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Up-regulated genes have higher mCH levels than down-regulated genes.
source: Plotting gene body mCH in wild-type mice for each category of differentially expressed genes, we find that, overall, DEGs have greater gene body mCH than genes that are unchanged, with up-regulated genes having higher mCH levels than down-regulated genes (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by gene body methylation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: mCG levels are higher on DEGs than non-DEGs for the majority of DEGs categories.
source: The same analysis showed that mCG levels are also higher on DEGs than non-DEGs for the majority of DEGs categories (Figure 4B), consistant with the idea that total methylation may also influence the final transcriptional outcome (Lagger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by gene body methylation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Total methylation may influence the final transcriptional outcome.
source: The same analysis showed that mCG levels are also higher on DEGs than non-DEGs for the majority of DEGs categories (Figure 4B), consistant with the idea that total methylation may also influence the final transcriptional outcome (Lagger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of higher mCG on DEGs and supported by citation.

claim: Loss of Dnmt3a dependent mCH and mCG significantly contributes to gene expression changes seen in the Dnmt3a cKO.
source: These analyses demonstrate that loss of Dnmt3a dependent mCH and mCG significantly contributes to gene expression changes seen in the Dnmt3a cKO.
evidence: This is supported by running average plots showing correlation between methylation loss and gene expression changes.

claim: mCH, but not Dnmt3a dependent mCG, plays a central role in mediating RTT pathogenesis.
source: Importantly we find that mCH, but not Dnmt3a dependent mCG, does in fact play a central role in mediating RTT pathogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by integrative analysis showing strong correlation between mCH loss and gene expression changes in common DEGs for Mecp2 cKO but not mCG.

claim: Conditional knockout of Dnmt3a in GABAergic inhibitory neurons leads to genome-wide loss of mCH.
source: Here we find that conditional knockout of the mCH writer, Dnmt3a, in GABAergic inhibitory neurons leads to genome-wide loss of mCH and a small subset of mCG sites, causing hundreds of gene expression changes to impair neurophysiology and behavior with some deficits mirrored in a matched deletion of Mecp2.
evidence: This is supported by methylation sequencing data.

claim: Conditional knockout of Dnmt3a in GABAergic inhibitory neurons leads to loss of a small subset of mCG sites.
source: Here we find that conditional knockout of the mCH writer, Dnmt3a, in GABAergic inhibitory neurons leads to genome-wide loss of mCH and a small subset of mCG sites, causing hundreds of gene expression changes to impair neurophysiology and behavior with some deficits mirrored in a matched deletion of Mecp2.
evidence: This is supported by methylation sequencing data.

claim: Conditional knockout of Dnmt3a in GABAergic inhibitory neurons causes hundreds of gene expression changes.
source: Here we find that conditional knockout of the mCH writer, Dnmt3a, in GABAergic inhibitory neurons leads to genome-wide loss of mCH and a small subset of mCG sites, causing hundreds of gene expression changes to impair neurophysiology and behavior with some deficits mirrored in a matched deletion of Mecp2.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Conditional knockout of Dnmt3a in GABAergic inhibitory neurons impairs neurophysiology.
source: Here we find that conditional knockout of the mCH writer, Dnmt3a, in GABAergic inhibitory neurons leads to genome-wide loss of mCH and a small subset of mCG sites, causing hundreds of gene expression changes to impair neurophysiology and behavior with some deficits mirrored in a matched deletion of Mecp2.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: Conditional knockout of Dnmt3a in GABAergic inhibitory neurons impairs behavior.
source: Here we find that conditional knockout of the mCH writer, Dnmt3a, in GABAergic inhibitory neurons leads to genome-wide loss of mCH and a small subset of mCG sites, causing hundreds of gene expression changes to impair neurophysiology and behavior with some deficits mirrored in a matched deletion of Mecp2.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral testing data.

claim: Some deficits in Dnmt3a cKO are mirrored in a matched deletion of Mecp2.
source: Here we find that conditional knockout of the mCH writer, Dnmt3a, in GABAergic inhibitory neurons leads to genome-wide loss of mCH and a small subset of mCG sites, causing hundreds of gene expression changes to impair neurophysiology and behavior with some deficits mirrored in a matched deletion of Mecp2.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of behavioral and physiological data between the two cKO models.

claim: Binding of MeCP2 to postnatal mCH contributes significantly to postnatal RTT symptoms.
source: First, binding of MeCP2 to postnatal mCH contributes significantly to postnatal RTT symptoms, but there still appear to be other genomic targets recognized by MeCP2 or other functions whose loss contributes to the disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that ~40% of Mecp2 cKO DEGs are also altered in Dnmt3a cKO and show strong dependence on mCH.

claim: There appear to be other genomic targets recognized by MeCP2 or other functions whose loss contributes to RTT.
source: First, binding of MeCP2 to postnatal mCH contributes significantly to postnatal RTT symptoms, but there still appear to be other genomic targets recognized by MeCP2 or other functions whose loss contributes to the disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that some Mecp2 cKO DEGs are not altered in Dnmt3a cKO.

claim: MeCP2 'reads' a subset of Dnmt3a dependent methylation sites to significantly impact gene expression.
source: Second, though MeCP2 'reads' a subset of Dnmt3a dependent methylation sites to significantly impact gene expression, there appears to be a much broader gene regulatory program set up by the placement of global mCH and some mCG via Dnmt3a.
evidence: This is supported by the finding that only ~12% of Dnmt3a cKO DEGs are also altered in Mecp2 cKO.

claim: There appears to be a much broader gene regulatory program set up by the placement of global mCH and some mCG via Dnmt3a.
source: Second, though MeCP2 'reads' a subset of Dnmt3a dependent methylation sites to significantly impact gene expression, there appears to be a much broader gene regulatory program set up by the placement of global mCH and some mCG via Dnmt3a.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that most Dnmt3a cKO DEGs are not altered in Mecp2 cKO.

claim: The phenotypes of whole-body knockout of Mecp2 are recapitulated in the brain-specific knockout.
source: First, while the phenotypes observed in whole-body knockout of Mecp2 are recapitulated in the brain-specific knockout (Chen et al., 2001; Guy et al., 2001), the phenotypes of whole-body (Okano et al., 1999) and brain-specific (Nguyen et al., 2007) knockout of Dnmt3a diverge, highlighting the essential role of Dnmt3a in peripheral tissues.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The phenotypes of whole-body and brain-specific knockout of Dnmt3a diverge.
source: First, while the phenotypes observed in whole-body knockout of Mecp2 are recapitulated in the brain-specific knockout (Chen et al., 2001; Guy et al., 2001), the phenotypes of whole-body (Okano et al., 1999) and brain-specific (Nguyen et al., 2007) knockout of Dnmt3a diverge, highlighting the essential role of Dnmt3a in peripheral tissues.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Dnmt3a has an essential role in peripheral tissues.
source: First, while the phenotypes observed in whole-body knockout of Mecp2 are recapitulated in the brain-specific knockout (Chen et al., 2001; Guy et al., 2001), the phenotypes of whole-body (Okano et al., 1999) and brain-specific (Nguyen et al., 2007) knockout of Dnmt3a diverge, highlighting the essential role of Dnmt3a in peripheral tissues.
evidence: This is inferred from the divergence of whole-body and brain-specific knockout phenotypes.

claim: Early deletion of Dnmt3a in the brain drives neurological symptoms.
source: In addition, while prior studies showed that early deletion of Dnmt3a in the brain drives neurological symptoms (Nguyen et al., 2007; Kohno et al., 2014), deletion of Dnmt3a using Cre-drivers that turn on postnatally have been demonstrated to produce minor (Morris et al., 2014) to no neurological symptoms (Feng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Deletion of Dnmt3a using Cre-drivers that turn on postnatally produces minor to no neurological symptoms.
source: In addition, while prior studies showed that early deletion of Dnmt3a in the brain drives neurological symptoms (Nguyen et al., 2007; Kohno et al., 2014), deletion of Dnmt3a using Cre-drivers that turn on postnatally have been demonstrated to produce minor (Morris et al., 2014) to no neurological symptoms (Feng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The underlying methylation pattern remains largely unaffected if Dnmt3a is deleted later in development.
source: Therefore, it is likely that the underlying methylation pattern remains largely unaffected if Dnmt3a is deleted later in development, precluding the evolution of deficits.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that postnatal deletion produces minor symptoms.

claim: MeCP2 phenotypes are observed regardless of when the gene is deleted.
source: This is in contrast to MeCP2, where phenotypes are observed regardless of when the gene is deleted (McGraw et al., 2011; Cheval et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Dnmt3a and MeCP2 have overlapping but distinct roles to produce functionally normal neurons and behaviors.
source: Our study deliberately eliminated these variations and shows that Dnmt3a and MeCP2 have overlapping but distinct roles to produce functionally normal neurons and behaviors.
evidence: This is supported by the comprehensive comparison of the two cKO models.

claim: Loss of mCG in Dnmt3a cKO is likely due to de-methylation in the embryonic brain that cannot be re-methylated in the absence of Dnmt3a.
source: The loss of mCG is likely due to de-methylation in the embryonic brain (Lister et al., 2013; He et al., 2017) that cannot be re-methylated in the absence of Dnmt3a.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of mCG loss and supported by citations showing embryonic demethylation.

claim: Loss of either Dnmt3a or MeCP2 leads to misregulation of hundreds of genes that normally have higher methylation (mCH in particular) relative to genes that are unchanged.
source: At the RNA level, we show that loss of either Dnmt3a or MeCP2 leads to misregulation of hundreds of genes that normally have higher methylation (mCH in particular) relative to genes that are unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and methylation data.

claim: Expression of genes misregulated in both cKO models changes in both the up and down direction in a manner that is independent of gene length.
source: We find expression of these genes changes in both the up and down direction in a manner that is independent of gene length.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis showing DEGs in both directions and analysis by gene length.

claim: The vast majority of the genes misregulated in both cKO models change to a similar degree and in the same direction.
source: Importantly, the vast majority of the genes misregulated in both cKO models change to a similar degree and in the same direction, consistent with equal dependence of these genes on Dnmt3a and MeCP2 for proper regulation.
evidence: This is supported by log2 fold-change correlation analysis.

claim: There is a significant contribution of mCH and mCG to the fold change in gene expression in Dnmt3a cKO mice.
source: Integrating our genomic datasets, we find a significant contribution of mCH and mCG to the fold change in gene expression in Dnmt3a cKO mice consistent with these marks functioning together to regulate gene expression during neuronal maturation.
evidence: This is supported by running average plots showing correlation between methylation loss and gene expression changes.

claim: mCH and mCG function together to regulate gene expression during neuronal maturation.
source: Integrating our genomic datasets, we find a significant contribution of mCH and mCG to the fold change in gene expression in Dnmt3a cKO mice consistent with these marks functioning together to regulate gene expression during neuronal maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between both methylation types and gene expression changes.

claim: There is a significant contribution of mCH, but not mCG to the misregulation of a subset of genes in the MeCP2 cKO.
source: Intriguingly, we see a significant contribution of mCH, but not mCG to the misregulation of a subset of genes in the MeCP2 cKO.
evidence: This is supported by running average plots showing correlation between mCH loss but not mCG loss and gene expression changes in common DEGs.

claim: Binding of MeCP2 to mCH is critical for the postnatal evolution of RTT symptoms.
source: This together with overlapping behavioral and physiological data suggests that binding of MeCP2 to mCH is critical for the postnatal evolution of RTT symptoms.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong dependence of MeCP2-regulated genes on mCH and overlapping phenotypes.

claim: MeCP2 is likely one of a number of functional factors interpreting Dnmt3a dependent methylation.
source: Our molecular data suggest that MeCP2 is likely one of a number of functional factors interpreting Dnmt3a dependent methylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that only a small percentage of Dnmt3a cKO DEGs are also altered in Mecp2 cKO.

claim: Re-analysis of single-nuclear RNA-seq datasets from cortical inhibitory neurons are consistent with the conclusion that MeCP2 is a restricted reader for Dnmt3a dependent methylation.
source: Though the overlap in gene expression changes between models has not been quantified until here, re-analysis of single-nuclear RNA-seq datasets from cortical inhibitory neurons (Stroud et al., 2017) are consistent with our conclusion (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by re-analysis of published data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The current model for Dnmt3a dependent gene regulation should be updated to incorporate that MeCP2 is a restricted reader for Dnmt3a dependent gene regulation.
source: With these data in hand we propose that the current model for Dnmt3a dependent gene regulation (Stroud et al., 2017) be updated to incorporate our insights that MeCP2 is a restricted reader for Dnmt3a dependent gene regulation, as well as that postnatal mCG plays a role in the epigenetic program driven by Dnmt3a during neuron maturation.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings of the study.

claim: Postnatal mCG plays a role in the epigenetic program driven by Dnmt3a during neuron maturation.
source: With these data in hand we propose that the current model for Dnmt3a dependent gene regulation (Stroud et al., 2017) be updated to incorporate our insights that MeCP2 is a restricted reader for Dnmt3a dependent gene regulation, as well as that postnatal mCG plays a role in the epigenetic program driven by Dnmt3a during neuron maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between mCG loss and gene expression changes in Dnmt3a cKO.

claim: There is a defined set of proteins in the mammalian genome that possess a methyl binding domain (MBD) and have been shown to bind mCH in vitro.
source: There is a defined set of proteins in the mammalian genome that possess a methyl binding domain (MBD) and have been shown to bind mCH in vitro (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2018.

claim: There are other proteins involved in transcriptional regulation that do not possess a classic MBD and are sensitive to the methylation status of DNA.
source: However, there are other proteins involved in transcriptional regulation that do not possess a classic MBD and are sensitive to the methylation status of DNA, with some validated in vivo (Luo et al., 2018; Kribelbauer et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2010; Lomvardas and Maniatis, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The DNA binding of many transcription factors is both positively and negatively affected by DNA methylation.
source: For example, the DNA binding of many transcription factors is both positively and negatively affected by DNA methylation (Kribelbauer et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2017), a phenomena that is not exclusive to mammals (O'Malley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The DNA methylation and histone modification machinery are intimately linked.
source: Further, the DNA methylation and histone modification machinery are intimately linked (Lomvardas and Maniatis, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lomvardas and Maniatis, 2016.

claim: Methylation written by Dnmt3a antagonizes polycomb complexes to modulate gene expression in the differentiation of neural precursor cells.
source: This link has been specifically shown in the differentiation of neural precursor cells, where methylation written by Dnmt3a antagonizes polycomb complexes to modulate gene expression (Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2010.

claim: The discovery that MeCP2 reads only some Dnmt3a dependent methylation marks lays the groundwork to uncover novel factors responsible for postnatal gene regulation that may be critical in setting up a mature, healthy mammalian brain.
source: All in all, our discovery that MeCP2 reads only some Dnmt3a dependent methylation marks lays the groundwork to uncover novel factors responsible for postnatal gene regulation that may be critical in setting up a mature, healthy mammalian brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: 95% of neurons in the striatum are inhibitory medium spiny neurons.
source: The striatum is ideal because mCH patterns are highly cell-specific and the vast majority of neurons (95%) in this region are inhibitory medium spiny neurons (Dudman and Gerfen, 2015; Kemp and Powell, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by citations.
